options: Well-formed: `hello` is found in `Base<int>` when `Derived<int>` is instantiated
Ill-formed: `hello` is not found, because unqualified lookup does not search the dependent base `Base<T>`
Ill-formed, no diagnostic required
Well-formed only because `Base<int>` is not explicitly specialized
questions.explanation: `hello()` has no arguments, so it is not a dependent call and is looked up in phase one. Unqualified lookup at the definition does not look into `Base<T>`, a dependent base, because a specialization of `Base` could have entirely different members. Nothing named `hello` is visible, so the program is ill-formed and GCC and Clang both reject it. Writing `this->hello()` or `Base<T>::hello()` makes the name dependent and fixes it.

questions.prompt: `use` fails to compile because `h.get<3>()` is parsed as comparisons. What is the correct spelling of the return expression?
options: `return typename h.get<3>();`
`return h.template get<3>();`
`return h.get template<3>();`
No change: since C++20 the compiler looks inside `H<T>` to see that `get` is a template
questions.explanation: `h` has a dependent type, so in phase one the compiler cannot know that `get` is a member template, and without help the `<` is a less-than operator; the original code is ill-formed. The `template` keyword after `.` tells the parser that the next name is a template. `typename` marks types, not templates, and C++20 relaxed only `typename` in type-only contexts and the lookup of unqualified template-ids, neither of which helps a member access.

options: `g(int)`
Ill-formed: the call `g(1)` is ambiguous
`g(double)`
It depends on the compiler
questions.explanation: `g(1)` has no type-dependent arguments, so it is not a dependent call: it is looked up and bound at the template definition, where only `g(double)` is visible. The later `g(int)` would be a better match, which is why `g(int)` is tempting, but it is never considered for this call. If the call were `g(T{})`, it would be dependent, though ordinary lookup would still see only `g(double)`, and argument-dependent lookup finds nothing for `int`.

Ill-formed: `size` is not found in `Base<T>`
questions.explanation: `size()` is not a dependent call, so it is looked up at the definition, and unqualified lookup skips the dependent base `Base<T>`. It finds the global `::size`, binds to it, and `n` returns 0. There is no ambiguity, because `Base<int>::size` is never a candidate. Without the global function, the program would be ill-formed as the last option says; with it, the bug is silent.

questions.prompt: Which of the two uses of `twice` are well-formed?
options: Both: `helper` is looked up at the point of instantiation, where both overloads are visible
Only #2
Neither: `helper` must be declared before the template
Only #1
questions.explanation: `helper(t)` is a dependent call. Ordinary unqualified lookup is done only from the definition context, where no `helper` exists, and argument-dependent lookup is done from both the definition and instantiation contexts. For `lib::X`, ADL searches `lib` and finds `lib::helper`. For `int`, there are no associated namespaces, so the global `helper(int)` declared after the template is never found and #2 is ill-formed. The first option describes a single lookup at instantiation, which is not the rule.

questions.prompt: How does a conforming compiler parse the statement in `q`?
options: As a declaration of `ptr`, a pointer to `T::type`
As a multiplication of `T::type` by `ptr`, which here is ill-formed because `ptr` is not declared
It is deferred until instantiation, when the compiler knows what `T::type` is
As a declaration in C++20 and later, because P0634 made `typename` optional
questions.explanation: A qualified name that depends on a template parameter is assumed not to name a type unless it is preceded by `typename`, so the statement is an expression: `T::type` times `ptr`. `ptr` is a non-dependent name and is undeclared, so phase one rejects the template. P0634 removed the need for `typename` only in contexts where a type is the only possible parse, and a statement in a function body is not one of them.

questions.prompt: In C++23, in which of these positions inside `template<class T> struct S { ... };` is `typename` still required before `T::value_type`?
options: `using V = T::value_type;`
`T::value_type member;` as a data member
`void set(T::value_type v);` as a member function parameter
`void f() { T::value_type local{}; }` inside a member function body
`auto g() -> T::value_type;` as a trailing return type
questions.explanation: C++20's P0634 defines type-only contexts in which a dependent qualified name is assumed to be a type: alias declarations, the decl-specifiers of member declarations, parameters in member declarations, trailing return types, named cast targets and a few more. A statement in a function body is not such a context, because `T::value_type local{};` could equally be an expression, so `typename` is still required there. All the other positions compile without it in C++20 and later.

questions.prompt: The function template `u` is never instantiated. What does the C++23 standard say about this translation unit?
options: Well-formed: templates are only checked when instantiated
Ill-formed, and a diagnostic is required
Undefined behavior
Ill-formed, no diagnostic required
questions.explanation: The initialization does not depend on `T`, and it would be ill-formed in a hypothetical instantiation right after the definition; no valid specialization of `u` can be generated either. [temp.res.general] makes such a program ill-formed with no diagnostic required. That permits early diagnosis without requiring it: Clang 21 rejects this translation unit, while GCC 16 accepts it, which is why the first option looks right on GCC.
